utterances.text: I'm actually more specifically referring to the -- I want to -- want you to tell me if your last answer was referring to the commander of the operations group, as opposed to the commander of the organic structure which you were within, because I'm directing it at the commander of the operations group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, my friend may be directing it at the commander of the operations group and he's made that pretty clear, but, Your Honour, the answer there looks pretty clear as well. Clarification is one thing, and attempts to try for what is now about the ninth time for the answer you want is another. I now object to this line of questioning continuing. It's pretty clear, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, to make the matter, you know, settled, I will allow the -- the ninth time try on this occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you understand that the clarification I'm seeking is in your last answer were you referring to the commander of the operations group at the time when the crime was committed or the commander of the 3rd Corps, for crimes committed by people within the operations group at that time? That's -- that's what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a crime is committed within the -- the OG, then it is the relevant units of the OG that deal with the crime or in terms of the superior command, it would be the command of the 3rd Corps, if the crime has taken place within the operations group that I was in command of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said earlier that on some occasions MUP units were subordinated to you from the Ministry of the Interior. If those MUP units had committed crimes whilst within your -- whilst under your command, who would have been responsible or investigating the crimes committed by them while under your crime in combat? Would it have been you or someone else?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be the one to instigate the investigation; however, the MUP bodies would be involved and they would be in charge of the investigation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] I am seeking a clarification here to be sure that I have understood you well. You have told us that Mr. Halilovic told you that his role was to coordinate the activities within combat operations on the ground. When he -- when did he tell you this?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he told me this at the first meeting in Jablanica or maybe on the way from Jablanica to Konjic, when we were in his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the meeting in Dobro Polje, did he repeat that phrase?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How did you understand this formula to coordinate combat activities on the ground? How did you understand -- how did you understand the meaning of that sentence?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way I understood it is that he had the authority to issue concrete tasks on the ground and to engage units in a very specific sense and that behind that idea there was the Main Staff or the commander of the Main Staff, Mr. Delalic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But in your view, who was it who was in charge of that operation? Who was the commander of that operation?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In very specific terms, I received my orders and I reported to Mr. Sefer Halilovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but you were convinced that Mr. Halilovic was the commander. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have any dilemmas as to his function. He was the Chief of Staff. However, I believe that in his capacity he was in the position to issue orders to me on the ground and I was duty-bound to report to him on the execution of his orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did he give you the explanation of his function? Why did he tell you that his role was to coordinate the combat? If somebody is a commander, does he have to explain his role? Why did he have to explain to you that he had this authority? Why did he say what he said to you, in your view? What was he trying to explain to you?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what his aim was. I believe that he wanted to explain his role to me as a participant in the previous operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But do you find it normal if it comes from a commander -- would it be normal for a commander to explain his role? Wouldn't it suffice for him to just exercise his authority? Did he feel the need -- why did he feel the need to explain what his mission entailed?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably Mr. Halilovic knows why he did what he did. I believe that at that time there was a lot of confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I am asking for your personal opinion. What did you yourself understand? How did you feel about this explanation?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at the time there was a lot of confusion about many things on the ground, amongst which one has to say that a few months before that Mr. Delalic [as interpreted] was appointed commander of the Main Staff, and I believe that among the soldiers on the ground there was certain confusion about the new role of the commander and the old role of the Chief of Staff, and the way I understood it is that Mr. Halilovic wanted to explain his situation to the commanders that he came in contact with at the time. In that sense, that's why he did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I apologise to interrupt. The transcript has twice said "Mr. Delalic." I think the witness actually said "Mr. Delic" and it won't be corrected in the transcript because we actually heard the words "Delalic." So if that could be corrected before we go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have heard the representative of the Prosecution. The name that you have mentioned, did you mention the name of Mr. Delic or Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I move to another topic that needs to be clarified. This is about what you have said with regard to the use of MUP forces. And you have explained that the -- it was up to the commander of that unit to agree upon that use with the -- the head of the local MUP. My question is as follows: In that particular case, the superior MUP officials, would they be aware of that fact or do you believe that the agreement between you as the commander and the head of the civilian police would be kept to yourselves?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that should be the case in principle. In practical situations there was often very little time. There were no communication means. So I believe that this was more often done in the direct contact with the local commander of the police and no official approval was sought from higher echelons of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you, however, notify your superiors? Was it possible that the units under your authority acted without informing your superiors about what is going on?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what happened in 1993. The situation changed somewhat in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. [In English] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge El Mahdi. I have some questions out of your questions. The first one is that: Witness, you told Judge El Mahdi that you sent combat reports to Mr. Halilovic. My question is that: Where could you be sent this report to and where could Mr. Halilovic be reached in the first half of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my IKM, I sent the reports to the command post of the 317th Brigade. I had the information that at this command post there was Mr. Suljevic and Mr. Bilajac, and they communicated over the communication means with Mr. Sefer Halilovic. I didn't know where Mr. Sefer Halilovic was at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course, you know, there is a so-called forward command post. Why don't you send your report directly to that post?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To whose forward command post?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So you don't know at all there is a forward command post in Jablanica during that time?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know that there was one, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the next question is that you testified Mr. Halilovic could issue orders in the spirit of general guidelines. Which guidelines are these?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to the active defence and the tasks that the units had to liberate the area. I am also referring to the orders issued by the Main Staff to individual units or commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, in your testimony you used the term "General Staff" and the "Supreme Command" on a number of occasions. Are these different organs within the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my understanding, the Supreme Commander was the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the Main Staff was its professional organ, which in technical terms engaged in combat and commanded the office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions out of the Judges' questions? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I just have one, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just arising out of a question His Honour Judge Liu asked you a moment ago about your awareness -- well, you said you didn't know there was a forward command post at Jablanica. The question is just this: How far away geographically or physically were you located from Jablanica in that period in September 1993?

utterances.speaker: SELMO CIKOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Physically, the distance was less than 100 kilometres; however, in order for me to reach Jablanica from my forward command post, it would take me two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No questions from Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: There are no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. At this stage, are there any documents to tender from both sides? Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could I just confer with my case manager. I'm just not sure whether one of the documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- I referred to is in evidence or is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, I understand that the three documents I referred to are already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Morrissey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, the Defence seeks to tender those documents that were offered for tender during the course of the cross-examination. I believe the ones that were only marked for exhibit -- marked for identification were military manuals 195, 196, 197, and then parts, I think, 198. Some of those were then broken up into parts as exhibits, 198 and 199 and 200 were separate pages. I'd seek to tender those -- those documents. I believe that our -- Mr. Cengic has provided a list of and copies of the documents that we promised yesterday, and also to the Prosecution. And I should indicate what my learned friend Mr. Re confirmed earlier on, that the Prosecutor have located a translation of one of those documents, and perhaps after discussion with the Prosecutor we can add that as an exhibit. But I won't do so now because I haven't cited it myself. And finally, MFI -- sorry, document D201 is in evidence. So it's really the military manuals that I offer and seek to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There's -- there's no objection. Could I just note that the translation -- or the documents we provided yesterday late to the Defence, one is the entire translation of the book "Rukovodjenje i komondovanje." That's the entire -- that's the -- that includes the three extracts which are MFI198, 199, and 200. So the Trial Chamber basically has the opportunity to have the three English translations before it almost immediately. We don't object to the tender of those documents, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your assistance. And those documents are admitted into the evidence, and our request to the Defence to submit all those documents to the registrar or to the court deputy of our case so that she could scan it into the system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, witness, thank you very much indeed for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. Madam Usher will show you out of the room and we wish you a very pleasant journey back home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as we decided that we still have some time, we would like to discuss about the submissions by the Defence yesterday. And I instructed both parties to meet after yesterday's sitting, and I want to know are there any positive results from those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to clarify, we are now referring to the -- the submissions commenced by Mr. Mettraux yesterday concerning the admissibility of certain documents through the witness Jusuf Jasarevic. Your Honour, we have complied with Your Honour's suggestion and we have discussed the matters, but in the event -- and I should say that with respect to some other documents which were not the subject of controversy yesterday but in the occasion of discussion, my learned friend and I have had some discussion, and there are other documents to be admitted by consent through this witness. As to the ones raised yesterday, Your Honour, I have to report that all of those documents which were foreshadowed as being objected to by my learned friend Mr. Mettraux, co-counsel, remain objected to, with the exception of one document, that is, D -- that is the document number 163, number 163. Now, could I indicate in short -- well, my learned friend will have more to say about this in a moment, but just so that the Court know -- the Tribunal know where is the controversy lies at this point, I can indicate this: With respect to the list provided by the Prosecutor, any document above 150 is objected to. And they are objected to on a number of grounds. The first ground on which they're objected to at this stage is the ground that these documents were provided late and were permitted to be added to the exhibit list by this Tribunal after objection by the Defence. The Tribunal considered the matters and ruled upon these matters. Leaving aside any proceedings that occur elsewhere, which are not appropriate really to concern ourselves with here -- would Your Honours just excuse me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I would -- I don't ask Your Honours to -- to make any finding about this, but you'll be aware that there's been an application made by the Defence with respect to that ruling. However, for these purposes we proceed on the basis, of course, that it's a binding ruling. Nevertheless, there's a remedy being pursued in relation to that. That is one reason not to admit them now at this point. Secondly, when the Chamber made its ruling there, it furnished the Defence with one residual protection, and that was the requirement that these documents be led at a later time. Now, that -- and I'm remaining now on matters of form rather than matters of substance, but they're important protections. That left the Prosecution with two possibilities: Either they could call this witness now and put the documents in through somebody else, or they could call this witness later. That was a choice that the Prosecution had, and that's really their decision. But it's a matter of prosecutorial convenience rather than necessity that this matter -- that these documents go in now. So that's the first matter that the Defence will raise. The second matter is -- and I won't go through these document by document now, because the Prosecutor should be allowed to say what they have to say first about that. But we can indicate that almost none of these documents ought to be tendered through this witness at all. Some of documents the Defence will say should not be admitted into evidence through any witness at all, and it will be the Defence position that most of them are -- they're not just hearsay; they're third-hand, fourth-hand, gossip, unverifiable rumours relating to periods of time that in the most is part have nothing so do with the indictment here. They're being led in essence to establish the notice of Mr. Halilovic, and what we'd submit is that they're not probative, they're not reliable, and they're not appropriate to this witness, so they're objected to on just about any ground that could be imagined. But we've got substantive arguments to mount about each document in respect to each of those matters. That's why the controversy exists. And I won't go into each document now. The Prosecutor can indicate what her position is. So that's the controversy that's before the Tribunal. Could I say something about how it might be appropriate to deal with it and what might be an efficient way. Because the objections taken by the Defence focus in substance upon the relevance and reliability on one hand but also on the suitability of this witness, Mr. Jasarevic, the forthcoming witness, it may be appropriate to notice that they fall into categories, these documents. Some of them are documents that come from the civilian police, as the evidence will reveal -- well, no speeches, but so that they're sourced with the civilian police. Some of them do appear to have passed through the office of this witness. In respect of those, a different position may be available. We argue the contrary, but so that the Court will be in a position to distinguish on the basis of that. Some of the documents may have been cited by the witness himself. The question of their relevance and reliability remains an issue, but those documents would be in a different category again, of course, because if he saw them or had good reason to see them, then they may be relevant to his evidence directly. So that that may be a logical way to proceed with these documents, rather than engaging in a -- a pre-trial trial where we go through each document at length with evidence, that seems to be inefficient and it's desirable to deal with this today if possible. So that may be a good way to deal with it. And I raise it as a possibility. My friend can respond as she sees fit. But the final issue that we would raise in terms of -- what our objections are is that we just haven't had a chance to test the reliability or the admissibility of many of these documents as we'd like to have. As I say, some of them are -- are -- the bulk of them are intelligence - and I use that term in the broadest possible tense - intelligence reports concerning what some people say another person said about Sefer Halilovic or in some cases about Ramiz Delalic and other people. They look on their face to be entirely untestable, but perhaps it may be that with the exercise of diligence we'll be able to find something that's relevant. And finding that may be directly relevant to whether it should -- whether the document should get in at all. And for those reasons, we'd be submitting that the chain of custody of these documents is not an idle matter. It's not simply putting the Prosecution over the -- over the jumps. It's a matter that may be relevant. Because in order to test these documents, we -- we may be able to find something and it will require some work to be done frankly in Sarajevo. That will have to be done. However, I -- I want to make this clear too, that I do not at this point have a clear plan as to how to deal with that matter. I can't say to the Tribunal, "If you give us a week, I'm going to send operatives there." So I don't want to pretend that that's the case. What I can say is that some of documents look on their face as if they need a bit of investigation, but I make that concession in advance. And, of course, the other thing is -- is about -- frankly, we -- as my friend indicated yesterday, we did rely on the court order in preparing for witnesses. It's true, the Prosecution point out they're not voluminous. And that is -- that is the fact. They're not voluminous. It's not their length that troubles us. It's the fact that we can't test them and that we frankly in recent times as Your Honours probably have noticed have been relatively busy and we don't just the time. It comes back to that problem, being exposed to the need to investigate like that in the middle of a trial. The Court makes its decisions on a variety of bases, but we are left with that problem that's posed by the late provision of material. And for that reason, we ask that the protection furnished in that order be maintained and we're going to object to all those documents, as I've indicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I have some questions concerning of your submission just now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned that you object to admit this document. What do you mean by that? You know, using a document in the courtroom is different with the admission of the document. Do you mean the using or its admission?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I mean both. I'm -- in relation to these documents, I mean the using as well. I'm sorry, I should have specified that. But I do mean -- that's a common-law habit. I apologise. We telescoped the two things into one. So I apologise for that. Yes, I do mean by -- I object to this witness being shown these documents, and frankly I object to them being shown to the Tribunal. And could I say this -- and this is in response to Your Honour's question. We appreciate that is this not a jury trial and we appreciate too that the Court consists of experienced and professional Judges who are well able to deal with - and I concede you are trained to and do - deal with material that may be prejudicial and set it aside. But when a weight of such material of a vague and untestable character is provided, it cannot be in the interests of the -- of the Defence and in the interests of justice. And although we -- we trust, of course, in the Tribunal and that you may give such materials no weight, but it will be part of my submission later, and I'll -- I'll put it in advance now that, this material comes essentially from the police and the political enemies of Mr. Halilovic. And you may well appreciate what it's going to say. Some of it's very -- well, I won't go into it. But, you know, there's material in there that we're very concerned by. And of course we know the Prosecutor is not trying to poison the mind of the Tribunal by elicit material. We know they would never do that. And we know that they would submit this material only for what they say is a legitimate reason. But we think it's very, very far fetched, this material. And when you look at it, Your Honours will no doubt see why that is, and you'll rule then. You have to be acquainted with its contents to some degree. But that's why we object to it being produced at all. We think it's really colour and movement rather than substance, and it's colour and movement that's deleterious to a fair trial and not probative of the matters that are before the Court. That's a matter for argument. The Prosecutor will put her arguments. And that's a long response to Your Honour's question, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: It seems to me that you are very, very familiar with the contents of these materials already.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: I can indicate I am very familiar with the contents of these materials. And am not embarrassed by their volume at all. I know what's in them. And we won't be prejudiced by their -- in that respect, we don't allege any prejudice as to not knowing what's in them. It's a question of proving what we want to prove about them that is a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And could -- could I hear the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The Prosecution intends to tender 22 -- or not tender. I'm sorry. I used the wrong word -- to show the witness 22 documents. And out of these 22 documents, Your Honour, 14 are the new ones. They are not huge documents, and my learned friend has already conceded that he's very familiar with these documents, so it's not the element of time. Now, if one would look at Your Honours' ruling, and your ruling said that we should introduce the documents at a later stage, Your Honour. We would invite this Chamber, Your Honour, to draw a distinction between tendering the documents and getting a witness to comment on the substance of these documents. And I would also respectfully submit, Your Honours that this is the late later stage that we talked about. Counsel has now indicated he's familiar, he's not prejudiced by the contents of these documents, and as a result there'll be no prejudice if we ask this particular witness to comment on the substance of these documents. Your Honour, I will also point you to the guidelines that you issued on the admissibility of evidence, and clearly, Your Honour, within the substance of that is that the rule is in favour of admissibility of documents, and your Chambers will then have the -- you will decide on the weight and the probative value. And if indeed during the course of this trial it came to pass that these are indeed not admissible because the Defence have come forward with some proof on this, Your Honours will then discard it and not give the weight that is needed. But this can always be done, Your Honour, as the -- as the trial progresses. There is no need for it to be decided here and now. So the Defence is quite capable of continuing with their investigations and coming up with whatever arguments they want on the admissibility or the lack thereof of these particular documents. Your Honour, this witness that we are going to call is an extremely senior witness. He's a very high-ranking officer. He was the chief of the military police. As such, he is the one amply positioned to comment on the information in these documents. To deprive the Prosecution of the opportunity at this time, it really renders this witness -- perhaps the evidence will not assist the Trial Chamber as much as it ought to if we were allowed to show these documents. The Defence, on the other hand, Your Honour, will be showing this witness their documents. Therefore, I do not think that the -- that the Chamber will be assisted with the evidence of this witness to come to the totality of the understanding of -- of what this witness is going to be saying. Your Honour, so far the -- the practice here in this particular case has been that such -- such documents have been used. And I showed a lot of them to the witness Gusic. And these were a similar category of documents. And if you look at your practice directions, Your Honour, at 6, it does say that there's no blanket prohibition on the admission of documents simply on the grounds that the purported author has not been called to testify or similarly that a document is unsigned or unstamped, et cetera. I mean, Your Honours are familiar with your own directions to us. And in accordance with those directions, we would submit, Your Honour, that it would be quite proper and would not be prejudicial to the Defence to ask the witness to comment on them. Your Honours are quite capable if, as I said, it comes to pass to disregard the comments of the documents itself. Your Honour, the Defence have also been introducing documents here which they -- which are plainly relevant, and even if the witness did not know of the particular document but can confirm whether the information contained therein is accurate and to their own knowledge that that's what they knew. Your Honour, one of the mains -- grounds my learned counsel raises is that they have not had the opportunity to test the reliability. Reliability is different to relevance, and they are -- have the opportunity as the trial continues to test it and bring forth to the -- to the -- to the Chamber. The other is the -- the other ground that the Defence counsel have raised is that they are not relevant. Now, the Prosecution would submit in that regard, Your Honour, they're clearly relevant documents. They are very relevant. They are in the time period. They're going to talk about a critical aspect of the Prosecution case theory, and a lot of the documents, as my learned friend has indicated, do point to the 9th Brigade and what the atmosphere was at the time and what was happening. This witness is clearly the one who can talk about it. Your Honours, we have cut down our Prosecution list dramatically. We don't have another witness at this seniority. The other security officers, Your Honour, are security officers of brigades and they will not be able to at the vantage-point that this particular witness is to explain and assist the Trial Chamber in arriving at the truth of the matter. Otherwise, Your Honours, it would be an extremely lopsided evidence as the Defence have been showing documents to which we have never been privy before, and it will prejudice the Prosecution -- I mean if the Prosecution is capable of being prejudicing, and its takes an extreme case, and I think this is the one. If Your Honour is so minded as to grant this, then perhaps we would request this Chamber that we -- that we retain the right to recall this witness or, indeed, the second answer may be that we don't call this witness at all. And since the -- the witness which was supposed to have been here as the next witness is not well, this will delay the proceedings, Your Honours. But the most important point, Your Honour, is your ruling said to be admitted at a later date, to be introduced. We are not introducing these documents, Your Honour. We are merely asking the witness to comment upon them. And it will be at a later stage. And I think this is the later stage, given the indications from counsel that he's very familiar with them. The prejudice was going to be caused by the fact that he was not familiar with them. There are only 14 new documents, Your Honour, and they were primarily from the ABiH archives. So, Your Honour, these would be my submissions in this regard, unless there's anything else I can assist Your Honours with. But we would insist that we show these documents to this witness so that he may comment on them. And they're extremely relevant and probative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I have one question to -- for the clarification that -- in your submissions, you mentioned that it is impossible to introduce those documents through other witnesses at a later stage. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I would not -- I would not say "impossible." I would say there would be some of these documents which we will be able to -- to introduce through another witness but just some, not all of them. But nevertheless, they do not have the -- the position that this particular witness has, as the chief of the military security. And some documents will not be. Some documents, he's not the author and not the addressee of. We freely admit that. But we would like to show the documents, as we did to Mr. Gusic, so he may comment on the information contained therein. So I will again, Your Honours, draw the distinction between producing the documents and showing the witnesses the document for their comments about the information. And yes, some of them are from the police. Some are from other organs. But it's vital for us that we -- we ask the -- this particular witness. So not all of them. That was -- I'm getting the habit from Mr. Morrissey in giving you a long answer to your questions. The short answer is although we could introduce some of them, but not all of them, but the prejudice to us is not allowing this witness to comment on them., not the production in itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, another question to Mr. Morrissey: That concerning with that witness, have you received the proofing notes submitted by the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I received those notes this morning. Can I indicate that I got a -- a phone call from my friend last night who indicated that she was proofing very cautiously in light of what she was being told, and I indicated to her that I understood that that was an appropriate course. So we make no complaint about any delay. The Prosecutor didn't delay. They have worked hard, up until late last night, as I understand the position, and it may be also this morning. We have received those notes at a relatively late time t Prosecutor has given us an explanation as to why, and frankly we accept that explanation completely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I do, Your Honour. With respect to that, the Prosecutor has got two real problems on this application. The first is that there's an order in place and it was an order designed to protect the Defence from the very problems that we're now facing. The Prosecutor seeks to evade that order by saying that the order related to the admissibility of -- of evidence, but in the end she corrected that to the introduction of evidence, and that was an appropriate change for my friend to make because it was the introduction of evidence that was the problem. Secondly, in respect of the MUP documents, the Prosecution are calling two individuals in this case. One is called Bakir Alispahic, who is featured in a colourful, short way in the evidence given last week; and the other is Enver Mujezinovic. Both of those are Ministry of the Interior people. Bakir Alispahic has the vantage-point, among other things, of being the Minister of the Interior at the time, so it couldn't be said that he was a mere brigade commander or lower. He was the Minister of the Interior. And Enver Mujezinovic was a senior officer at that time. We've got other objections to these documents, of course, but they're objections relating to the individual document. But at a general level, when you're calling the Minister of the Interior, that's the person through whom to put Minister of the Interior documents. And in my submission, there's no basis at all for suggesting that the Prosecutor would be embarrassed by not putting those documents to that witness. Your Honours, it is the fact that the Prosecutor is entitled to try to prove the notice of Mr. Halilovic. That's an element of the offence they've got to prove. So of course they're entitled to do that, and I don't want the Prosecutor to misunderstand what our objection is. We say that these documents are not capable of doing that. The evidence of the witnesses may be relevant to that fact, and those witnesses can be asked about the relevant facts within their knowledge. Should they need -- and they should be asked that orally in court. And then if they need to refresh their memory from documents that they brought into being, yes. Furthermore, if there are expert documents or documents within their competence that are brought into being, then of course even if they don't remember them or didn't see them, then, as with this witness and as with Mr. Gusic, they can be shown those documents and to comment on them in a relevant way. But you can't get one -- an expert in eggs to comment on expertise about oranges. This man who's coming now is a military security chief. He's not the head of the military police. That's not his position. He's the head of the SVB, the military security service. That's a distinct organ within the army. The Minister of the Interior is the police, the civilian police. They're quite different. They're organically different. They're under different ministries and I don't think there'll be any challenge to this, frankly. So that my friend hits the hurdle -- both that there's an order in place which she hasn't, in my submission, explained a reason for departing from, and secondly, that there are people through whom these documents should be tendered, if they're otherwise relevant. This witness here, I indicated there's an argument to be mounted which is a sensible one that if this witness -- if the document passed through the witness's hand, it may be appropriate to show him. But this MUP material really should not even be shown in proofing. It's -- after 11 years there's a real danger in showing witnesses things that they had no idea at the time, didn't see, and they are then shown this to refresh their memory. You know, there's a clear danger in doing that and frankly I'm -- I'm a bit concerned about it. But whatever the propriety to have that may be, it doesn't need to be done in court, it doesn't help this Tribunal. You want to hear the evidence of that witness and that's what you should hear, not something that comes from another branch of the government which he may not ever have seen or had reason to see. So I won't go to the specifics of each document now. That really arises on a document-by-document basis and you don't need to deal with all those in that way now. But that's my response to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, it seems to me that the two extreme views between the parties and the issue has not been solved after yesterday's meetings between the parties. I believe the Defence raised their objections for the using of those documents on two reasons: The first one is the late submission; the second one is that they believe that the witness will not be the right witness to put these documents to. As for the second reason, the Trial Chamber has very serious doubts on that because we are still in the Prosecution's case. Whatever documents they use, it's their strategy. And only after using these documents could the Trial Chamber be in a better position to know whether this document is relevant or not, whether this witness is the right person or not. So I'm afraid that we cannot agree with the second reasoning on that particular issue. The first reasoning, that is, the late submission, as the Defence counsel rightly pointed out, we made a ruling on the 14th of February, 2005 to this aspect, and we believe that it is in the interest of justice and in full respect of the rights of the accused that Defence should have adequate time to prepare properly for trial, which includes the examination of the exhibits the Prosecution intends to use during the trial. Since we have already made a decision subject to any decisions contrary to it, no matter in this Bench or in the Appeals Chamber, this decision should be respected and abided by by both parties, as well as this Bench. But, however, there might be some way for manoeuvre according to this stage because we said that the new exhibits should be used at a later stage. We did not specify the period. I mean, what is the later stage? There's no definition on it. So under those circumstances, I would like to know whether it's possible for us to hear this witness next Monday. So during the weekend, this afternoon, and tomorrow, the Defence will have enough time to consult with their client and to discuss this issue. Yes, Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: It's possible that that delay would remove the objection raised as to being embarrassed by timing. I would be clear that we maintain our objection to the admissibility of the documents, but it is true that if we had that time, that would allow us to consider whether there was a particular line of examination that needed to happen. And to that extent, that would palliate the element of surprise and lateness which has been raised, and I agree that would be of benefit in that regard. I have to clear that that would not cause us to withdraw our objection to the introduction or admissibility of -- of the evidence, but it may be relevant to Your Honours' consideration of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Is it agreeable to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. CHANA
utterances.text: We're in Your Honours' hands in this matter, your, -- Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: May I just raise one matter there? My learned friend Mr. Weiner raised a possibility yesterday constructively, and we don't know whether it's in Your Honours' hands to help us, but it may be that if Your Honour gave an indication, that would help us in dealing with the authorities elsewhere. Could we indicate that we would like to opportunity to visit Mr. Halilovic on the weekend at some point. And if Your Honour were to indicate that that may expedite and speed up the trial proceedings, then such a comment from the Bench might assist the authorities to make their decisions. And I wonder if Your Honour would be prepared to give such an indication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. And so we decided that we'll hear the next witness next Monday by using all the documents proposed by the Prosecution, which does not mean that we have to admit them. We'll consider that during the proceedings and after the proceedings. Another consideration is that the proofing notes provided to Defence in a very short notice, we also would like to give enough time for the Defence to study that proofing notes on the next witness. At the meantime, I will do my best or maybe issue an instruction or order to the registrar concerning with the visit during the weekend, which means Sunday or Saturday, for the Defence team to have the access to their client to discuss all the matters involved in those new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's so decided. Mr. Morrissey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORRISSEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I just indicate that we will endeavour to see Mr. Halilovic tomorrow in any event, since we have that opportunity. So we'll stay in touch with the authorities about that. And yes, we're grateful for the indications. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, another issue is that we understand that the Defence filed the application for certification. Now we are waiting for the response from the Prosecution on that issue. Are you going to respond on that issue or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As the Court know, we have seven days. I know they're working on it right now and it should be ready today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed. And by the way, the so-called Gusic decision concerning of the document will be rendered after this sitting. Are there any other things that the parties would like to mention at this stage? I see none. So the hearing is adjourned, and we'll see you next Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of February, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25
